stem: Explain Darwin's theory of natural selection.
solution:
Charles Darwin proposed the theory of natural selection in his book 'On the Origin of Species'. Its main points are:
1. Overproduction: Every species produces many more offspring than can survive.
2. Struggle for existence: Because natural resources (food, space, mate) are limited, there is a constant struggle for survival among individuals.
3. Variations: Individuals of a species show small variations; some variations are favourable and some are not.
4. Survival of the fittest: Individuals with favourable variations are better adapted to the environment, so they survive and reproduce, while the less-adapted ones are eliminated. Nature thus 'selects' the fittest — this is natural selection.
5. Inheritance of favourable variations: The favourable variations are passed on to the next generation. Over many generations these accumulate, gradually giving rise to new species. This process is called evolution by natural selection.

stem: Write the factors affecting the environment.
solution:
The factors affecting the environment are of two types:
1. Abiotic (non-living) factors: air, water, soil, temperature, sunlight (light), humidity, rainfall, pressure and minerals.
2. Biotic (living) factors: plants (producers), animals (consumers), and micro-organisms (decomposers), and their interrelationships.
In addition, human activities such as deforestation, urbanisation, industrialisation and pollution greatly affect the environment. All these factors together determine the ecological balance of an environment.

context: Refer to the figure of a hydroelectric power station showing the reservoir wall with three marked levels — A (top), B (middle) and C (bottom) — the sluice gate, penstock, turbine, generator and power house.
stem: With reference to point B, the potential energy of how much water in the reservoir of the dam will be converted into kinetic energy?
solution: The water flows out to the turbine through the intake/penstock at level B. Therefore only the water lying above the level of point B — i.e. the water column between point B and the free water surface at the top (level A) — has a head above the outlet, and it is the potential energy of this water (the water above point B) that gets converted into kinetic energy as it rushes down the penstock to the turbine.
figureNote: Cut-section diagram of a hydroelectric dam/power house with reservoir levels A, B, C marked on the wall, sluice gate, penstock, turbine, generator, power house and transmission towers, p-06.

context: Refer to the figure of a hydroelectric power station showing the reservoir wall with three marked levels — A (top), B (middle) and C (bottom) — the sluice gate, penstock, turbine, generator and power house.
stem: What will be the effect on electricity generation if the channel taking water to the turbine starts at point A?
solution: Point A is near the top of the reservoir. If the intake channel starts at A, the height (head) of the water column above the intake is very small and only a little water is available above that level. Hence the potential energy, and therefore the kinetic energy of water reaching the turbine, will be low. As a result the turbine rotates slowly and electricity generation will decrease (be much less).
figureNote: Same hydroelectric dam cut-section figure with levels A, B, C, p-06.

context: Refer to the figure of a hydroelectric power station showing the reservoir wall with three marked levels — A (top), B (middle) and C (bottom) — the sluice gate, penstock, turbine, generator and power house.
stem: What will be the effect on electricity generation if the channel taking water to the turbine starts at point C?
solution: Point C is at the bottom of the reservoir. If the intake channel starts at C, the entire column of water above C (the maximum head of water) is available, so the water has maximum potential energy which is converted into maximum kinetic energy at the turbine. The turbine rotates fast and the electricity generation will be maximum (highest).
figureNote: Same hydroelectric dam cut-section figure with levels A, B, C, p-06.

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 2
stem: Cockroach, Frog, Sparrow, Star fish — from these animals, which one can regenerate its broken body part?
solution: Star fish can regenerate its broken body part. If an arm (and part of the central disc) of a star fish breaks off, it can grow back a complete new body, i.e. star fish shows regeneration. Cockroach, frog and sparrow do not regenerate lost body parts in this way.

stem: Complete the diagram showing the various processes (steps) in tissue culture.
solution:
The steps of plant tissue culture shown in the cyclic diagram are:
1. Explant: a small piece of plant tissue (e.g. from a bud/shoot tip) is taken from a healthy plant.
2. Culture in nutrient medium (sterile flask/bottle): the explant is placed in a sterile nutrient medium containing plant hormones.
3. Callus formation: the explant divides repeatedly to form an undifferentiated mass of cells called callus.
4. Shooting and rooting: the callus is transferred to another medium where it differentiates and develops shoots and roots, forming tiny plantlets.
5. Transplantation of plantlets: the plantlets are transferred to pots/soil, where they grow into complete new plants.
figureNote: Cyclic diagram of plant tissue culture with several blank boxes and images (mother plant, callus, culture bottle, box labelled 'Shooting and Rooting', plantlets), to be completed, p-07.

stem: Which fuels are obtained from biomass?
solution: Fuels obtained from biomass include: (1) Biogas (mainly methane, from gobar gas plants), (2) Bio-ethanol/ethanol (from fermentation of sugarcane molasses and other plant material), (3) Bio-diesel (from vegetable oils/plant seeds), and (4) solid biomass fuels such as firewood (wood) and charcoal. These are renewable fuels produced from plant and animal matter.
